summary: Kole Jain walks through seven website design trends he considers underused at the end of 2024, as an alternative to the bento layouts and 3D animations he sees everywhere: text swapping, hand-drawn UI marks, text treated as a visual element, line dividers, morphing images or videos, animated diagrams, and images inside navigation menus. Each trend is shown on real sites, with a short note on what makes it work, such as the contrast between crisp bold text and loose hand-drawn marks, or rounded edges on dividers. He adds a few practical warnings: check font licenses, don't use lines on everything instead of spacing, and keep morphing-image changes small so the animation doesn't stutter. For a design system, the video is a menu of expressive options for landing pages and marketing sites, each of which could be offered to a person as a visual choice rather than a default.
key_ideas: Bento layouts and 3D animations are everywhere in 2024 websites; less common effects make a site feel more original.
Text swapping shows two matching pieces of text in one spot, which makes a simple, text-only page feel interactive with little work.
Hand-drawn circles, underlines and arrows over crisp, bold text create a striking contrast.
Text can be a visual element that tells a story, not only paragraphs, especially with a distinctive font or animation.
Fonts taken from other websites need their licenses checked before use.
Line dividers are coming back, but lines on everything instead of spacing feel like old PowerPoint slides.
Dividers don't have to be straight lines everywhere; rounded edges can work well.
Morphing images or videos can spice up weak media and make an entrance or a reel more striking, but massive image changes can slow the browser and make the animation choppy.
Animated diagrams can explain a multi-step process as the visitor scrolls, or respond to hover in a simpler version.
Images in a navigation menu help visitors tell products apart when the product names don't explain themselves.
Even photos that aren't specific to menu items make a dropdown menu more engaging than plain text.

rules.rule: On a text-led landing page, consider swapping a line of text for a matching alternative in the same spot as the visitor scrolls.
rules.why: It shows two matching kinds of text in one spot and makes a simple page interactive without much work.
rules.evidence: really cool way to have two matching kinds of text in one spot

rules.rule: When adding hand-drawn circles, underlines or arrows, set the surrounding text in crisp, bold type so the loose marks contrast with it.
rules.why: The contrast between perfect bold cut text and hand-drawn, slightly blurred handwriting is what makes the effect catch the eye.
rules.evidence: the contrast between this perfect bold cut text and then the handdrawn

rules.rule: Check a font's license before using a font file found on another website.
rules.why: The source warns that without care over the licenses you will be a real criminal, not just joking about copying.
rules.evidence: you do need to be a little bit careful about the licenses

rules.rule: Treat text as a visual element with a distinctive font or animation, instead of relying only on plain paragraphs.
rules.why: Text can become an element that tells a story; distinctive and animated fonts are a strong way to do this.
rules.evidence: your text doesn't just need to be boring paragraphs

rules.rule: Don't put lines on everything as a substitute for spacing sections apart.
rules.why: Lines everywhere recall old PowerPoint slides where people didn't realise they could just space things apart, and cramming content between lines looks dated.
rules.evidence: when people didn't realize that they could just space things apart

rules.rule: If you use line dividers, consider giving them rounded edges rather than straight lines everywhere.
rules.why: The source shows rounded-edge dividers working well on Isomorphic Labs.
rules.evidence: you can add some rounded edges to them

rules.rule: Make sure the changes in a morphing image aren't massive.
rules.why: Massive changes can slow down the browser and make the animation seem choppy.
rules.evidence: make sure the changes to your image aren't massive

rules.rule: Consider morphing an image or video when the media is weak on its own and needs spicing up.
rules.why: The source presents morphing as a great way to spice up an image or video that is not strong enough alone.
rules.evidence: you need to spice it up a little

rules.rule: To explain a multi-step process, consider a diagram that reveals each step as the visitor scrolls, or a simpler diagram that animates in and reacts when each item is hovered.
rules.why: Scroll-driven diagrams let visitors see the whole process in depth, and hover diagrams are a simpler but still interactive alternative.
rules.evidence: as we scroll down we get to see the whole process in depth

rules.rule: When product names don't explain what the products are, show an image of each product in the navigation menu.
rules.why: Visitors can tell products apart at a glance, as with Rivian's truck and SUV, like pictures on a restaurant menu.
rules.evidence: they should do this on all websites or at least more of them

rules.rule: Consider adding photos to dropdown menus even when they aren't tied to a specific item.
rules.why: A menu that is only text is dull; photos add something to it.
rules.evidence: when this menu comes down normally it's just text

decisions.question: How should sections be separated: visible line dividers or space alone?

options.name: Straight line dividers
options.effect: Clear section boundaries; can feel rustic or modern depending on execution, but lines on everything look like old PowerPoint slides.
options.when: When visible structure suits the style, as on the source's deliberately rustic cookie site or its modern cryptocurrency site.

options.name: Line dividers with rounded edges
options.effect: Softer divisions that still mark sections, as on Isomorphic Labs.
options.when: When straight lines feel too harsh for the rest of the style.

options.name: Space only
options.effect: Sections separated by spacing, with no lines.
options.when: When lines would crowd the layout; the source notes people once added lines because they didn't realise they could space things apart.

decisions.recommendation: The source says line dividers are coming back and growing on him, but warns against using lines everywhere or jamming content between them.
decisions.evidence: line dividers are kind of coming back into style

decisions.question: Should the page use hand-drawn marks (circles, underlines, arrows) over its text?

options.name: Hand-drawn marks over bold text
options.effect: Loose, slightly blurred handwriting and arrows contrast with crisp, bold type; can carry a hover animation.
options.when: For a simple landing page built mostly from text, since the source says it is easy to put together.

options.name: No hand-drawn marks
options.when: When the effect doesn't fit the brand [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: The source calls hand-drawn effects a really cool effect that is easy to put together and growing on him, though he admits there is a little more to it than he describes.
decisions.evidence: handrawn effects are definitely the way to go

decisions.question: How should headline text behave on the page?

options.name: Plain paragraphs
options.effect: Standard text blocks; the source calls repeated paragraphs boring.
options.when: When content, not display, is the focus [inferred].

options.name: Distinctive display font as an element
options.effect: Text becomes a visual element that tells a story.
options.when: When the page can carry an expressive font [inferred], and only if the font's license allows the use.

options.name: Animated text
options.effect: A distinctive font that animates out into other shapes or content.
options.when: When the page wants a moment of motion built from type.

options.name: Text swapping
options.effect: Two matching pieces of text alternate in one spot, often on scroll.
options.when: For a simple, text-only page that should still feel interactive.

decisions.recommendation: The source favours treating text as an element, with distinctive or animated fonts, rather than boring paragraphs.

decisions.question: Should hero images or video reels morph as they enter?

options.name: Static media
options.effect: Images and videos appear without shape changes.
options.when: When the media is strong on its own or performance matters most [inferred].

options.name: Morphing media
options.effect: The image or video changes shape as it enters or moves, and can slide into large text.
options.when: When the image or video needs spicing up, or for a reel or portfolio entrance, making sure the changes aren't massive.

decisions.recommendation: The source likes morphing entrances but says to keep image changes small so the browser doesn't slow down.
decisions.evidence: morphing images or videos is a great way to do things

decisions.question: How should a multi-step process or diagram be presented?

options.name: Static diagram
options.effect: The full diagram is visible at once with no animation.
options.when: When there is no time to build an animated version [inferred].

options.name: Scroll-driven animated diagram
options.effect: Each step is revealed as the visitor scrolls, walking through the process in depth.
options.when: When the team has the time and patience to build it; the source calls it very time-consuming.

options.name: Animate-in diagram with hover
options.effect: The diagram animates in; hovering each item makes it rotate around and blur things out.
options.when: When a simpler but still interactive version is enough.

decisions.recommendation: The source calls the scroll-driven version among the most impressive effects but very time-consuming, and the hover version a simpler, still interactive option.

decisions.question: Should the navigation menu include images?

options.name: Text only
options.effect: A plain list of names; the source calls this no fun.

options.name: Product images per item
options.effect: Each item shows a picture of the product, so visitors can tell them apart at a glance.
options.when: When product names don't explain what they are, as with Rivian's R1T and R1S.

options.name: General photos in the dropdown
options.effect: Photos that aren't tied to a specific item make the dropdown more engaging.
options.when: When the menu drops down and would otherwise be only text.

decisions.recommendation: The source says more websites should show images in navigation, citing Rivian as doing it best.

caveats: Opinion-led, self-described satirical trend roundup published 2024-12-21; the trends reflect the presenter's taste, not measured results, and some may have dated.

The video suggests saving font files from other sites through the browser's developer tools, framed with the copy-versus-steal saying; it warns about licenses, and this practice conflicts with using only properly licensed fonts [inferred].
Jokes about lazy or untalented designers are humour, not guidance.
Self-promotion at the end: a Discord community with over 13,000 members.

Several names come from auto-captions and are uncertain: 'division by neural', 's.org', 'we are motto', '1 nil.com', 'develop medicines', 'Kiara Hoffer'. 'minam' is Minh Pham and 'rivan' is Rivian (matched to the description links and product names). The description's last link ('https://toyf') is truncated.
Nearly all examples are marketing, portfolio or shop websites, so these trends fit landing pages more than product UI [inferred].
The presenter says he neither has the time nor patience to build the scroll-driven diagram, and is unsure whether one divider example fits its cryptocurrency theme.
